title: Discovery of nuclear fission
summary: In December 1938, bombarding uranium with neutrons at the Kaiser Wilhelm Institute for Chemistry in Berlin-Dahlem, Otto Hahn and Fritz Strassmann found radioactive barium among the products: the uranium nucleus had burst. In January 1939 Lise Meitner, who had fled to Sweden, and her nephew Otto Frisch explained it with the liquid-drop model as a split into two fragments releasing huge energy, and Frisch named it nuclear fission. The discovery opened the way to nuclear energy and led directly to the atomic bomb.

uncertainty.note: Hahn and Straßmann identified radioactive barium on 19 December 1938; Meitner and Frisch formulated the theoretical explanation in Sweden over Christmas 1938 and published it in January 1939.

as_recorded.value: Nuclear fission was discovered at the Kaiser Wilhelm Institute for Chemistry in December 1938... On 19 December 1938, they arrived at an unexpected conclusion: Hahn and Straßmann showed, with the help of special chemical separation and analytical methods, that the reaction products observed were radioactive barium isotopes
Hahn s most spectacular discovery came at the end of 1938 when, while working jointly with Fritz Strassmann, Hahn discovered the fission of uranium

where.modern_name: Kaiser Wilhelm Institute for Chemistry (now Hahn-Meitner-Bau, Free University of Berlin), Thielallee 63, Berlin-Dahlem, Germany
where.historical_name: Kaiser-Wilhelm-Institut für Chemie, Berlin-Dahlem, German Reich

importance.justification: Opened the nuclear age of atomic weapons and nuclear power (R4 D3 T2 L4).

related.because: The discovery of nuclear fission demonstrated the feasibility of an explosive nuclear chain reaction, prompting the Allied race to develop the atomic bomb.

beats.caption: Otto Hahn and Fritz Straßmann detect barium isotopes from neutron-bombarded uranium in Berlin.
Lise Meitner and Otto Frisch provide the theoretical physical explanation of nuclear fission.
